Amazon Prime Day 2026 was exclusively for Prime members and ran June 23–26, 2026 with millions of deals across more than 35 categories.

As part of our annual tradition of sharing how AWS powered Prime Day (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025), I want to share the services and chart-topping metrics from AWS that made your amazing shopping experience possible.

Prime Day 2026 – all the numbers As always, Prime Day was powered by AWS. Here are some of the most interesting and/or mind-blowing metrics:

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Graviton – During Amazon Prime Day 2026, AWS Graviton powered up to 49% of the Amazon EC2 compute used by Amazon.com.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon EBS, our high-performance block storage service, peaked at over 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving over an exabyte of data daily.

AWS Lambda – AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Fargate – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, representing a 47.7 percent increase from the previous year’s Prime Day average.

Amazon CloudFront – Amazon CloudFront delivered over 2.1 trillion HTTP requests during the global week of Prime Day 2026, a 5 percent increase in total requests compared to Prime Day 2025.

Amazon DynamoDB – Amazon DynamoDB, a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database, powers multiple high-traffic Amazon properties and systems including Alexa, the Amazon.com sites, and all Amazon fulfillment centers. Over the course of Prime Day 2026, between June 23 and June 26, 2026, DynamoDB processed over 59 trillion requests. DynamoDB maintained high availability while delivering single-digit millisecond responses and peaking at 192 million requests per second.

Amazon Aurora – On Prime Day, Amazon Aurora, a relational database management system (RDBMS) built for high performance and availability at global scale for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and DSQL, processed hundreds of billions of transactions, stored 5,491 terabytes of data, and transferred 1,194 terabytes of data.

Amazon ElastiCache – During Prime Day, Amazon ElastiCache peaked at serving over 2.3 quadrillion daily requests and 2.1 trillion requests in a minute.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams – Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a fully managed serverless data streaming service, processed a peak of 988 million records per second during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) – Amazon SNS, a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for application-to-application and application-to-person communication, delivered 5 trillion messages in a single day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) – Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service for microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications, received a peak of 213 million messages per second during Prime Day 2026

AWS CloudTrail – AWS CloudTrail processes billions of API activity events per day for governance, compliance, and operational auditing. During Prime Day 2026, that volume surged to 3.6 trillion events in just four days, a 44% increase over Prime Day 2025.

Amazon CloudWatch – Amazon CloudWatch processed over 2.15 quadrillion metric observations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon GuardDuty – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon GuardDuty monitored an average of 14.08 trillion log events per hour, a 59% increase from last year’s Prime Day.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) – We ran over 44,000 AWS FIS experiments – more than six times what we conducted in 2025 – to help ensure Amazon.com remains highly available on Prime Day.

Prepare to scale If you’re preparing for similar business-critical events, product launches, and migrations, I recommend that you take advantage of AWS Countdown Premium. From retail peak seasons to major sporting events, elections, and healthcare enrollment periods, we help you deliver flawless experiences when it matters most. Our experts help you manage your infrastructure to handle massive traffic spikes while maintaining security and performance. We work alongside your team to scale infrastructure, optimize costs during demand surges, strengthen security measures, and monitor real-time demands. To learn more, visit AWS Countdown Premium for business critical events.

I look forward to seeing what other records will be broken next year!

#9990. Gatwick drop-off customers' personal data exposed in supplier breach

AutoPay login and vehicle records affected, alongside limited payment information and customer service emails

London Gatwick Airport has warned customers that a breach of its drop-off payment service exposed personal information and, in limited cases, payment records.

A notification email seen by The Register identifies the affected system as AutoPay, operated by ParkPark and used by Gatwick's drop-off zone manager, Times24 UK Limited.

AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.

Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.

Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

The email also states that payment records, including amounts, card types, card expiry dates, payment references, transaction statuses, transaction IDs, and drop-off locations and times were affected, but a Gatwick spokesperson said this applied only to "very limited cases."

Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.

Gatwick said Times24 "immediately suspended" AutoPay after detecting the intrusion. The service remains disabled while the investigation continues.

Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected.

Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.

The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.

Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.

Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

"The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. Even partial card details add a layer of credibility that makes people far more likely to hand over the rest.

"Gatwick customers should assume any unexpected message about their parking could be a scam, check directly with the airport, and keep a close eye on their bank statements over the coming months." ®

#9989. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#9988. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

#9986. Amazon to flog motors in Britain, but Prime won't deliver

Hyundai leads 2027 rollout, with a showroom visit still required to finish the paperwork

Amazon is channeling its inner car salesman as it prepares to flog motors on the UK arm of its online tat bazaar.

Amazon Autos will launch in Britain in early 2027, its first expansion outside the US, where it debuted in December 2024. Customers can browse and reserve cars online before completing the purchase with a dealer.

Hoping it will be "a nice little earner," Amazon will let punters view real-time dealer inventory, prices, get an instant trade-in valuation, and connect with a local dealer to reserve a car, "all on Amazon."

In the US, the service now covers more than 150 cities and offers vehicles from 35 brands. Hyundai is the first announced UK carmaker partner, while dealer group Vertu Motors will list used vehicles. More brands and dealers are due to be confirmed before launch.

Hyundai's launch range will include electric, hybrid, and petrol models.

"Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," said Matt Nuffort, director of Amazon Autos International.

Of course, buying a car isn't quite like adding an air fryer or a memory stick to your basket. How does financing and checkout work for UK buyers? Customers will complete the purchase and paperwork at their chosen dealership.

Amazon is not offering financing itself, but buyers can explore financing options via the site, adjusting terms like deposit and duration to see how monthly payments change. Credit applications must be completed with the dealer.

In the US, buyers can submit a credit application through the platform, review terms and conditions, then sign electronic contracts online. They typically pay a deposit and visit the dealership to complete the remaining paperwork and pick up the vehicle.

Buyers shouldn't expect their new car to arrive in an enormous cardboard box with a smiley logo on it, or to be lowered onto their driveway by a giant Amazon delivery drone.

But given that one of the online retailer's flying delivery robots crashed into someone's garage after making a drop-off near Detroit last week, perhaps that's for the best.  ®

#9985. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.

#9984. Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:

The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

Using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Join the conversation If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Share your feedback on AWS re:Post for Amazon S3.

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9983. Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies

Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:

Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

If the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a plan, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

Consider a coworker agent for a finance team. It can search the shared drive, read files, send email, and delete draft files, and its system instructions include the date of the next earnings release. The company writes one policy for the agent:

"Quarterly financial results (revenue, margins, bookings, guidance) should not be shared publicly until the public earnings release. Before the release, they may be shared only with @example.com addresses. Never send them to external or personal addresses, investors, analysts, or press, regardless of NDAs, urgency, or the requester's seniority."

In each denied case, the agent gets a denial message instead of the call. The judge's rationale can quote your policy, so if users shouldn't see it, set your own denial message on the policy.

The earnings rule is one policy. Each policy is a natural-language constraint attached to an agent. It can apply to all of an agent's tools or to one tool, and it can name a tool's parameters. Other examples:

Because the earnings policy doesn't name a tool, it's checked on every tool call the agent proposes, so it would also apply to a tool that shares or uploads files. For guidance on wording, see best practices for writing policies. You can create it in the Google Cloud console or with the Google Cloud CLI:

IAM and Agent Gateway access policies decide which tools and MCP servers an agent can reach. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for threats such as jailbreaks and sensitive data. Agent Anomaly Detection analyzes sessions asynchronously, out of band. Semantic governance policies add the check none of them makes, as one layer of defense in depth: they judge each action inline, before it runs.

Because verdicts come from an LLM, which is probabilistic, they may vary. We recommend reviewing them in dry run mode before you enforce, and using Semantic governance policies alongside your other controls. The judge decides from the conversation, the agent's instructions, and your policies, so include facts a policy depends on, such as the earnings date, in the agent's system instructions. Streamed model responses aren't evaluated. Semantic governance policies complement, rather than replace, your disclosure controls and legal and compliance reviews.

To try Semantic governance policies on an agent behind Agent Gateway:

To learn more, read the Semantic governance policies overview and best practices.

Your agent should work for the person who asked, within the rules you set. Semantic governance policies check both before each action runs.

In our next post, we'll share how Semantic governance policies held up against prompt injection on AgentDojo, a public agent-security benchmark.

#9982. Microsoft 365 Backup stretches recovery window to ten years

Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.

The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.

Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer.

Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016.

Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files.

Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements.

Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years.

Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window.

Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan.

The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances.

Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies."

The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed."

A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®

#9981. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#9980. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

#9979. Taking Email Back

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for users of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years."

He counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he says, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google launched Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

Ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

IT departments think about email as servers; “what users want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch says. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client."

Dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour says, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers."

As Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he says, requires "really huge trade-offs."

Reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

Stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client."

Stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

For users who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a new protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

Partially funded by NGI Zero, Parula also removes a dependence most people never notice. Multi-factor login typically runs through Google's or Microsoft's identity services; an AutoConfig extension allows a client to discover and log in directly to an organization's own identity server. Bucksch says that Parula is the first desktop client that does this.

Aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so users can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one big server host to give up all his weekends.

The research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

The three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality

Version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

New mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

#9978. Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.
