#9950. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9949. Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized dent in asteroid Dimorphos

Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage

The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original plan called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission launched in 2024.

DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision.

Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same.

"Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width."

Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit.

Hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits.

The plan is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer."

Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing.

Scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts.

Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet." ®

#9948. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9947. Make the Plan a Value

I recently finished adding support for idempotency tokens to amazonka (the unofficial Haskell AWS SDK), using the client token support provided by AWS. Implementing this required making some fairly substantial changes to the generator, the bespoke Haskell program that turns the service definitions in botocore into cabal packages. amazonka is over a decade old, and the generator has evolved as AWS have added new styles of APIs for their different services. Some services return XML, some return JSON, some return raw bytes, some return additional information in HTTP response headers, and so on. As a result, the generatorâs logic had been extended each time and had grown gnarly.

To untangle things, I resolved to make one of my favourite programming moves, âmake the plan a valueâ or âdecide what to do, and then do itâ. This move decouples two parts of a program by introducing an intermediate data structure (a âplanâ, or a value of a âplan typeâ) describing what is to be done before any action is taken.

I really like this pattern because the âdeciding what to doâ part of a program is often more complicated than the âdoingâ part. Separating the two often turns the âdecidingâ part into a pure function that produces a plan, making test cases simpler to write. And then if the âdoingâ phase is also complicated (because of remote API calls, rollbacks, parallel execution, or whatever else), itâs more manageable because those complications are not entangled with the planning logic. You also get to add a --dry-run flag almost for free, which is really useful for testing. (Henrik observes that testing for a dryRun variable everywhere pollutes the code somewhat. I think if he split his code into a planning phase and consumed that plan with either a âdry runâ printer or a ârealâ executor, the inline checks that he dislikes would disappear.)

This technique isnât subtle or obscure. Iâve seen it called the plan-execute pattern, and the ârouting slipâ enterprise integration pattern is literally about centralising the decision logic before execution. Iâve previously called it a âtiny DSLâ, and Matt Parsons sells its benefits in his Three Layer Haskell Cake article:

Having resolved to introduce a plan type, how do we work it into a venerable program like the Amazonka generator? For this part of the generator, it means separating the analysis of the loaded service definitions from the generation of the instance AWSRequest declarations. I did this by introducing a Config record of simple data and a function instanceD :: Config -> Decl () that builds Haskell code from that config record.

I found the generatorâs logic too difficult to understand and replace in a single change, so I replaced it incrementally using the strangler fig pattern. The most complicated part of this change was response parsing, so I added to the Config record an enumeration of ported response parsers, and a fall back to âdo things the old wayâ for everything else:

One thing that makes Amazonkaâs generator rewarding to hack on is that the service bindings act as an extensive and automatic golden test suite. Any changes to the generated bindings show up in diffs, and so if there are no diffs and the generator doesnât crash, the change probably didnât break anything. This makes the process of replacing the entangled code relatively simple (not easy):

The end result worked well and kept the individual commits readable (example: factoring out status code parsing). Adding the idempotency machinery was then straightforward.

The data types in the Amazonka example represent parameters to a Haskell code template, but this refactoring also works for more expressive plan types, such as âtiny DSLsâ, âlists of commandsâ, or âfree structuresâ. The trick is to keep a âdo it the old wayâ constructor in your plan type until the âold wayâ has been refactored away.

A well-chosen plan type introduces a narrow waist that decouples producers and consumers of your plan type, and the most obvious wins come from introducing alternate consumers of the plan: things like testability, --dry-run, and simpler executors all follow from that. A less obvious benefit is that you can also analyse and transform the plan itself. This is a great place to add pre-execution sanity checks or access controls. I regret that my tiny DSLs post inverted a transformation by interpreting it as matrix multiplications and inverting the result; it would have been simpler to provide an invert :: [Transform] -> [Transform] function.

Introducing alternate producers of the plan type can also pay off, but needs a bit more imagination:

âMaking the plan a valueâ works well in any language, but Haskellâs laziness makes it especially nice. Lazy evaluation can avoid materialising the whole plan in memory if it is consumed right away. Even in strict languages, the decoupling benefits are great enough that the extra memory use is often worth it.

#9946. AWS Weekly Roundup: Local Zone in Bogotá, 30-minute Lambda timeout, and more (November 24, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does. AWS Lambda launched in 2014 with a 60-second timeout, moved to 5 minutes in 2015 and to 15 minutes in 2018, and then stayed there for eight years. Last week the limit doubled, and in the same week Lambda learned to run on GPUs and gave platform teams their own runtimes. That is a lot of Lambda for one week.

Two other threads ran through the week. A new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá brought AWS infrastructure closer to users in Colombia. And AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), Amazon Cognito, and Amazon CloudFront each shipped a piece of identity for agents: who an agent is when it shows up at your door, and how little it should be allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a new Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia. AWS Local Zones place compute, storage, and networking near large metropolitan areas with the same APIs and tools as a Region, for workloads like real-time gaming, live streaming, and financial transactions. The Bogotá Local Zone supports Amazon EC2 C7i, M7i, and R7i instances, Amazon EBS gp3, gp2, and io1 volumes with local snapshots, Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Direct Connect, and Application Load Balancer. To start, enable us-east-1-bog-1a in AWS Global View.

AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute timeout for on-demand Event Functions – You can now configure any Event Function with a timeout of up to 30 minutes (1,800 seconds), double the previous limit, for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also go to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and event source mapping invocations keep the 90-minute timeout from September. Standard Lambda pricing applies, in all commercial Regions. Agentic requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, and file conversion are the workloads AWS calls out. Before raising the value, read the considerations in the Compute blog post: a service that invokes your function synchronously applies its own timeout, client read and socket timeouts need to be longer, and a NAT gateway drops idle connections after 350 seconds, so long calls need keep-alives. For longer work, durable functions still run for up to a year, and now emit OpenTelemetry traces.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances – You can now run GPU-accelerated inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing as Lambda functions, packaged as OCI container images, with no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile. In the walkthrough, four concurrent requests shared one copy of the model on a single GPU and finished in about the same time as one. It’s optimized for inference with custom models, on G-series instances from G4dn to G6e. You pay the EC2 instance fee (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply), a 9.75% management fee for GPU instances, and $0.20 per million requests.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon Polly now supports voice cloning – You can now create a custom voice in Amazon Polly from a few minutes of recordings of a consenting speaker, running on the Polly generative engine. It launches in seven languages, including English, Spanish, and Portuguese, and each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. Polly doesn’t keep the recordings or train on them. Creating a voice is free, and you pay for the speech you synthesize. It’s a gated release, so request access through your account team. The ML blog post covers brand-voice use cases for contact centers, voice agents, and content.

AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes – You can now manage a Lambda runtime as its own resource, separate from function deployment. Platform teams package approved SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring agents as an OCI image in Amazon ECR, and functions pick up updates as Lambda recycles execution environments, with no per-function redeploys. Updates can be staged, with health metrics and rollback. There’s no additional charge, and the Compute blog walkthrough shows the platform-team workflow.

AWS STS announces GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions at runtime – You can now take the temporary credentials a workload already holds and derive narrower ones, cutting permissions, session duration, or both. The result keeps the caller’s original identity, and permissions only ever narrow, so a sub-agent can never end up with more access than whoever created it. Access to the API is controlled with IAM policies, and every call lands in AWS CloudTrail. It’s available in all commercial Regions and beyond, including GovCloud (US) and China.

Amazon Cognito now supports dynamic client registration – You can now let MCP clients and AI agents register themselves at runtime (RFC 7591) instead of creating an app client in advance for each one. You choose between requiring an access token with a registration scope or opening registration to any client, and dynamically registered clients carry a client ID prefix so you can filter and manage them with the rest. It’s available on the Essentials and Plus plans, and client ID metadata documents arrived the same week.

Amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls – You can now call your own APIs from a function with cf.fetch() and act on the response, so authorization, personalization, or fraud checks that used to need Lambda@Edge or a trip to the origin can run at the edge. AWS’s own example: check an AI agent’s permissions and usage budget before the request reaches your API or MCP server. Network calls cost $0.10 per million on top of invocation charges and are included in the Pro flat-rate plan and above. The Networking blog post also covers cf.beacon() for background analytics.

Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports multi-Region peering across continents – You can now build a multi-Region Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster with peers on different continents, such as US East (N. Virginia) and Europe (Ireland), and read and write to one strongly consistent database from both. It was a busy week for DSQL: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures arrived, and storage upgrades brought up to 50% higher write throughput at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers – With more than 12,500 developers in R&D, BMW treats governance as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop, mostly in the CI/CD pipeline, so neither the agent nor its prompts can override it.

AI coding agents on Amazon EC2 Mac: How Cognition scales Devin for macOS – Cognition starts a fresh macOS VM for each Devin session in under a minute on Amazon EC2 Mac hosts across six Regions. The detail worth stealing: sessions are decoupled from hosts, and Cognition reports that about 90% release their VM when idle and resume from a snapshot in seconds.

How Klaviyo processes 3 billion daily events at scale with Amazon MSK Express – Timely reading for Black Friday week. Klaviyo moved from RabbitMQ to Amazon MSK Express brokers to absorb roughly 7 times normal event volume during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Running one set of processors across three priority topics, instead of separate infrastructure per level, cut costs by roughly 30%, according to the team.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – It’s next week: join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, or register for the free livestream to follow the keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9945. Huawei and crew tout homegrown EDA tools to overcome China’s fab deficit

Chip design software leans heavily into 3D packaging and multi-node assemblies

Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.

EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips.

Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools.

The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear.

Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology.

This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the company’s efforts to bring new EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy.

“Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he said.

We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area.

The TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It currently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process.

For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025.

So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms.

“Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He said. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics issues called for new analysis tools.”

This, He says, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live.

The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market.

We previously discussed the company’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. Many of these advancements will depend on multi-die chip packages, enabled by EDA tools, like those built by Phlexing. ®

#9944. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇

#9943. The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought

And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in

American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.

The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23.

It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020.

However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted.

Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords.

The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers.

According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17.

Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique:

The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22.

These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented.

Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo.

“Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

#9942. Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

The dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

An alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

This reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

There is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below shows.

To make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

We applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

The 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

The practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

The accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

The takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

Making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

The headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other."

Results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section says the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

You're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

The comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

#9940. The sky was once full of stars, kids; then the FCC let Elon Musk launch a million datacenter satellites

Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense

The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s plan to launch a million datacenter satellites.

The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”

The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the company to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union.

SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less.

Elon Musk’s company asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.”

The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request.

“SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The company must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters.

Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions.

Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “peak insanity.”

Google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily launches, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so.

Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create.

Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant new fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained.

Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites.

Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having launched a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029.

Down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India currently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here. ®
